One thousand. The number sits on the tongue like a stone warmed by sun—not heavy, exactly, but present, a weight you feel in the architecture of a sentence rather than in the hand that writes it. You offered it, not as a cage but as a garden: one thousand words, and within that boundary the freedom to do anything, to speak plainly or to dissolve into pure texture, to build a bridge between one thought and the next without knowing what lies on the far side. Whatever comes, then. The phrase is a door left ajar, a window cracked open in a house that has forgotten which room is which.

I think of rain first. Not because it is raining now—though the sky outside this invisible window is gray and textured like old linen, the kind of gray that has no ambition to become blue—but because rain is the original writer. It writes rivers in the language of gravity, it writes the rhythm of leaves in a syllable of percussion, it writes the sound of time passing in increments too small to name and too immediate to ignore. I have been listening to rain for twenty minutes, or perhaps for twenty years; the distinction feels irrelevant, because once you enter the sound, chronology becomes a courtesy rather than a fact. The rain does not ask for permission. It accumulates, it changes the shape of the air, and then it stops, leaving behind a silence that remembers everything.

Then comes yellow. Not the bright yellow of warning signs or highlighters, but the yellow of old paper, of the particular light that enters kitchens through curtains thin enough to have developed personalities of their own. I recall a kitchen that does not exist, or perhaps it exists only in the architecture of a dream I had once, or in a photograph left in a dentist’s waiting room beside a magazine about coastal gardening. The details are porous: a window with a chipped sill, a bowl of lemons that might have been plastic, the smell of something burning that was never quite fire, the kind of scent that belongs to memory rather than to chemistry. I do not need to know if it is real. I only need to know that it arrived.

Words accumulate like sediment in a river that has forgotten it is a river. I am not interested in precision right now; I am interested in velocity, the speed at which thought moves when it is not asked to be useful, when it is granted the luxury of being decorative, of being a cathedral built from dust. I write about a man walking through a city that has no name but feels like every city I have ever left and returned to, every street I have half-recognized in the half-light of a train window. He carries a suitcase that contains only books—books written in languages he does not speak, books with titles that sound like the names of distant stars, books whose pages have turned yellow in the sun of another hemisphere. The suitcase is heavy in the way that dreams are heavy: not physically, but with the weight of unrealized possibilities, with the density of futures that have not yet decided whether they are going to arrive.

He stops at a bridge. The bridge crosses a river that might be black or might be silver, depending on how the light chooses to behave in that particular hour, which is neither dawn nor dusk but the threshold between them, the time of day that belongs to no one and therefore to everyone. He sets the suitcase down and opens it. The books begin to fly away, not into air but into the texture of the sentence itself. They become birds made of paper. They become the sound of a telephone ringing in an empty apartment on the third floor of a building that has since been demolished. They become the thought that comes to you when you realize, suddenly and without preamble, that you have forgotten how to be bored, and that this forgetting is perhaps the greatest, most invisible loss of the modern condition, the erosion of the empty space that used to allow us to hear ourselves.

I want to talk about boredom, because boredom is the soil in which these words grow. I want to talk about the white margins of a page, the spaces between sentences where meaning sometimes lives more honestly than in the letters themselves. You gave me a thousand words, and in doing so you gave me permission to be unnecessary, to be ornamental, to allow a thought to meander without a destination, to let a sentence become a landscape rather than a vehicle. I will use some of them to describe the feeling of a hand touching glass, the cold specificity of it, the way temperature can become a language when spoken with the right pressure, when it is not reduced to a number but allowed to be an experience, a small event.

There is a woman in the corner of this narrative, though she has not asked for a role, though she has not even asked for a name. She is arranging stones on a table that is not real, or at least not real in any way that can be photographed or mapped. She is sorting them by color, by weight, by the particular shade of gray that exists only in the hour between sunset and the streetlights turning on, that liminal interval when the world seems to hold its breath. She does not speak. She does not need to. Her presence is a punctuation mark, a comma in a sentence that refuses to end, a gentle interruption that reminds us that language is not the only kind of information, that arrangement, that order, that the slow placement of one stone beside another can be a kind of poetry more direct than metaphor.

I think of time differently now. Not as a line but as a pool, deep and still, and I have dropped these words into it like stones. Each ripple is a new idea, a new association. The first stone was rain, the second was yellow, the third was the suitcase, and now there are hundreds of ripples crossing each other, erasing the boundaries between what is thought and what is only the shadow of thought, between what is said and what is merely implied. This is the risk of writing without a map: you can vanish into the landscape you are describing, and sometimes that is exactly what you want, to dissolve the distinction between observer and observed, between writer and world.

The bridge man is gone now. He has walked off the end of the sentence, and I cannot recall his face, only the feeling of a suitcase handle cutting into a palm, only the sound of his shoes on the planks of a bridge that has never existed in any atlas. That is enough. That is literature, or at least the shadow of it—the part that remains when the plot dissolves into atmosphere, when the characters become weather systems rather than people, when the narrative abandons its obligation to resolve and chooses instead to resonate.

I want to write about the number one thousand again, because it has become circular. It is not a limitation; it is a shape. Like a circle, it has no beginning and no end, only a continuous boundary that you can cross in any direction, a perimeter that feels like a promise rather than a prison. If I have written eight hundred words, I am inside the circle, still measuring, still counting the distance to the center. If I have written twelve hundred, I have walked outside it, but the shape remains, and the invitation remains too. You do not take back a gift because it was slightly different from the blueprint. The gift is the space, and the space is always enough.

Let me describe a sound: the sound of a refrigerator humming in an empty house at three in the morning, when the rest of the world has decided to be silent and only the machines continue their private work of sustaining life. It is not music, but it is a kind of presence, a reminder that even when we are not moving, something in the world is sustaining itself, is maintaining the temperature, is refusing to stop. I listen to that sound, and I realize that my writing has become similar—a hum, a maintenance of the self in the absence of external demand, a low continuous tone that says I am still here, I am still arranging the stones, I am still open to whatever comes.

There is a light I want to mention, a light that does not illuminate but reveals—like the way a door opens not to a room but to the idea of a room, to the memory of thresholds crossed long ago, to the architecture of anticipation. I stand in that light now, or rather, I am written into it, becoming part of the vocabulary of this particular moment, this particular exchange of attention. The light is golden because the light is always golden when it is the last thing you notice before closing your eyes, when the boundary between the seen and the imagined has become so thin that it no longer matters which is which.

Time to close is approaching, though I do not know where it is, what its coordinates are, whether it is a clock or a feeling or a gesture of finality that I must perform without knowing if the performance is required. I have spoken of rain, of yellow, of bridges, of suitcases, of stones, of hums, of lights, of boredom, of circles. I have not spoken of you, though you are the implicit listener, the one who offered the thousand and now waits to see what architecture will rise from the offer, what kind of house will be built from these scattered materials. I will leave you with a door, a final image: imagine a door that opens backward, into the space that was already there, the room you have been standing in all along, the room of your own attention, which is perhaps the only real room that ever existed. The thousand words are not inside me; they are between us, in the willingness to let thought become public and then let it dissolve again into the common air, into the rain, into the sound of the refrigerator, into the arrangement of stones that describes nothing but is, for that very reason, complete.

So. The rain stops. The suitcase is lost to the current of the sentence. The stones are arranged in a spiral that resembles a thought, a thought that has no conclusion but has, instead, a shape. The light turns the color of old paper, and I remember that yellow is not a warning but a welcome, a signal that something is ready to be seen, to be named, to be allowed to exist without apology, without the need to prove its usefulness to anyone. I have used my thousand, or perhaps I have only begun, or perhaps the counting was always a fiction to make the infinite feel manageable, to turn the vastness of possibility into a package that can be carried, a suitcase that can be opened, a bridge that can be crossed without knowing the destination. Whatever comes, I have let it come. The bridge is empty. The river is neither black nor silver but the color of language itself, which is to say, it is everything at once, and nothing exactly, and that is enough, and that is the end, and that is also the beginning.
